And last of all Toshizō,
with a "Hah!",
leapt atop the earthen wall and sat himself cross-legged on its roof-tiles.
A zip,
a zip,
and rifle-rounds grazed past his ears.
The corpsmen waiting inside the magistrate's office were aghast at Toshizō's recklessness.
"Vice-commander, what are you doing? Do you mean to make yourself a target for the Satsuma-Chōshū guns?"
"Hijikata-san—"
Harada Sanosuke and the others stretched up and seized hold of Toshizō's sash.
"You mean to die on us? If even you take a bullet, what's to become of the Shinsengumi?"
"Harada-kun,"
said Toshizō, jerking his chin toward the eighteen men of the Second Unit under Nagakura Shinpachi, already dashing out down the road,
"those men are out in the bullets too,"
he said. It was the usual hateful, immovable set of this man's face.
(Do as you please.)
and Harada let go his hold.
Toshizō sat there sprawled cross-legged.
(It's all theater.)

so he was thinking. A fight was one great piece of theater, staked on a man's life. It was precisely because Toshizō's own two eyes were watching that the death-braving Second Unit found its work worth the doing; and the men waiting within the compound too,
(If it is for this general...)
they were bound to think.
In truth Toshizō was no ordinary man. A born brawler to begin with, these several years he had passed, quite literally, through a forest of bared blades.
The vanity of the warrior is death.
That vanity had soaked to the very marrow of his bones and made his flesh and blood; there was something in it, one felt, that had built up the brazen face Toshizō wore.
Just then a roof-tile shattered.
Toshizō kept his usual hateful face. He had none of the "charm" that would make a man change color; as for charm, of any kind whatever, Toshizō had not a scrap.
Oddly enough, the bullets too seemed to want no part of this surly man, and every one of them flew wide.
(They ain't going to hit me.)
It was the confidence peculiar to a brawler. Toshizō's backside sat solid and heavy upon the roof of the earthen wall.
Meanwhile, out in the road, Nagakura Shinpachi's drawn-sword party had come to a savage pass.
The front assigned to the Shinsengumi was a thin wood commonly called the Shizuki-an grove, and there the Satsuma-Chōshū troops had raised a strange sort of rampart.
They had piled up tatami mats requisitioned from the townhouses, and, using them for a breastwork, poked their gun-muzzles through.
Through the wood the tatami breastworks were cleverly sited here and there, so that even if the position were broken into, there was no blind angle anywhere.

Cut down the gunners at one breastwork, and the man who charged in would at once be shot from another. For a field-position thrown up in a single night, it was truly well made. It was said to be by Chōshū's instruction: thanks to having been on the receiving end of the shogunate's Chōshū expeditions, the Chōshū clan had grown rich in the experience of siege and field warfare.
From the magistrate's office to that position was barely thirty meters, and less.
Toshizō picked out Nagakura and the other men finely drilled in the blade,
"Cut your way in,"
he ordered, and at the same time had the single field-gun the Shinsengumi possessed fire without a pause, to cover them.
Nagakura and the rest ran, swinging their bared blades.
They ran for their lives.
"Run!"
Toshizō roared from atop the wall. Unless they ran, they would be shot down before ever they reached the enemy line.
"An umbrella, we need an umbrella—"
said Harada Sanosuke, poking up just his head over the wall.
"An umbrella for what?"
said Toshizō.
"A bullet-warding umbrella. Rain you can keep off with one paper umbrella, but bullets won't have it that way."
Out in the road, corpsmen were falling one after another.
Take a bullet and the body leapt up before it fell. He fancied he could hear, even from here, the dull thud of each man dashed to the ground.

Nagakura sprang into the pine wood. After him five men, six men sprang in, but each clung to a single pine and could not stir a step; to move was to be shot from the tatami ramparts scattered all about.
Even so, Nagakura was making ready to dash out.
"Nagakura, hold! Don't you move."
Toshizō bellowed.
Having bellowed, he turned back to Harada within the compound,
"Pick fifteen men out of your unit,"
he said.
Harada made his choice at once, and one after another they climbed the two-ken earthen wall and leapt out into the road.
Toshizō too leapt down.
"Follow me,"
and as he ran he drew the two-shaku-eight-sun Izumi-no-kami Kanesada. In the instant he drew, a bullet struck the striking-edge of the blade with a sharp crack and glanced away.
"Run! Keep running!"
It was a fight in which running was the whole of the battle; there was no more to be said of it.
The bullets came on like rain. And at every five paces or so of that running, the shells the Satsuma gunners were firing from the Gokō-no-miya went
boom,
boom,
bursting on the road. The shells were packed with grape, so where they split open a mist of blood went up here and there.
Toshizō at last flung himself into the pine wood and took a single pine for a shield.
He looked back: the corpses in the road already numbered twelve.
"None of you rush out,"
said Toshizō.
They would wait for night. It would need, perhaps, only ten minutes more for the dark to come down full.
In a night action they would use the sword.
At close quarters the Shinsengumi were a name that rang through the realm.
(I'll build them a mountain of corpses.)
Toshizō had the confidence for it.
The front gate of the magistrate's office.
Here was the main body of the shogunal army, holding the magistrate's office for a fortress: the Aizu troops under that same old Hayashi Gonsuke as their commander.
Old Gonsuke, with three guns, first had fire opened on the Satsuma gun-position atop the Ryūunji heights.

But for every single round he fired it was as though ten came down in return; there was nothing his firepower could do, and moreover, from the wall of the Gokō-no-miya twenty meters before his eyes, the Satsuma riflemen were pouring in a wild fire.
"Guns on our side too—guns,"
old Gonsuke urged on the Aizu gunners; but, as it happened, too many of their guns were matchlocks.
They took a fearfully long time to work, and their effective range was one chō at the very most.

The Satsuma-Chōshū men were armed with the Minié rifle. In those days the Satsuma clan had machine-tools set up both at home and at its Kyoto residence, and nearly all its guns were of the clan's own making. Those guns had been handed over to the Chōshū army as well, free of charge, and in performance they were scarcely inferior to the foreign-made article.
As for guns, too, Ōyama Yasuke—who was at that very moment commanding the battery on the Ryūunji heights—had himself remodeled Western field-pieces, going so far as to make
what were dubbed "Yasuke guns,"
and things of that sort.
In those days, for the fighting strength of clan troops, Aizu and Satsuma were called the strongest in the realm; but in the matter of modernization the two would not bear comparison.
Aizu's art of war was still the hoary old Naganuma school, not a whit advanced since the age of the warring states.
It was new and old, then, that had collided.
Gonsuke at last dragged the three Aizu guns out onto the road at the eastern end of the magistrate's office and, at high elevation, fired them up at the Ryūunji heights.
The shells mostly burst against the pines, and the enemy position that mattered was not crushed.
Still, they had some little effect: a splinter grazed the earlobe of the second battery's commander, Ōyama Yasuke. The earlobe, and no more. The Satsuma gunfire only grew the brisker.
The Satsuma riflemen who had been shut up in the Gokō-no-miya now spread out too—into the road, under the eaves, behind the little wayside shrines—and began pressing slowly southward.
Old Gonsuke, directing from the road,
"It's a sword-charge now,"
and, spurring on his sword-and-spear men, he charged several times; but before they had gone even ten meters the vanguard had every one been made a corpse by the bullets.
Even so, Gonsuke charged as many as three times. But before and behind, to left and right, it only made more dead.
Gonsuke would not bend even then.
"Come—we'll push once more,"
and as he raised his long spear, three bullets pierced his body all at once.
He came down hard on his backside.
He could not rise.
When his men lifted him up to draw him to the rear,
"Don't touch me,"
he brushed them off, and, seated there in the road, went on directing the fight.
Night came.
Toshizō gathered every man of the Shinsengumi into the pine wood and set light to a single torch.
"Listen now: this flame is me. Follow the direction this flame goes."
The clusters of tatami redoubts within the pine wood had fallen silent. With the dark come down, they could no longer see a target.
"Harada-kun,"
Toshizō whispered in his ear.
Harada Sanosuke had a big voice.
Just as Toshizō had told him, he roared it from the pit of his belly toward the enemy in the pine wood.
"Listen, now—"
he bawled, and then, taking a breath,
"a thousand men of the Shinsengumi are charging in!"
This shout had its effect, sure enough.
The enemy felt a dread at the very sound of the word "Shinsengumi." The foe in this pine wood was mainly Chōshū's Second Infantry.
They began firing off wildly, at random.
"Guns fired in the dark of night,"
and Toshizō, marking where the muzzle-flashes came from, fell on them with a rush.
He cut.
Toshizō alone, four men.

Harada Sanosuke and the others fought till their spears broke, and at last the enemy gave way and scattered. On the Chōshū side at this point, casualties came to more than twenty, the platoon commander Miyata Hanshirō among them.
The enemy fled north.
North was exactly where the enemy's headquarters lay, the Gokō-no-miya that Toshizō meant to strike.
"Follow,"
and Toshizō, torch held high in his left hand and the Izumi-no-kami Kanesada aloft in his right, charged down the road.
He came to the eastern end of the magistrate's office.
The main body of the Aizu clan was there.
"What's become of Hayashi-san?"
"Over there."
an Aizu soldier pointed, and there sat Hayashi Gonsuke in the road, still in his armor.
He was directing the guns' fire yet.
"Ah—Hijikata-san, is it?"
old Gonsuke laughed.
A shell burst close beside his laughter, but Gonsuke did not so much as change color.
"It seems they've got you,"
"Musket-balls,"
he said, pointing to his left arm, his hip, his right knee,
"lodged in me. And you—not yet?"
"Not yet."
and as he said it, a bullet came flying and shot the torch out of Toshizō's hand.
Slowly taking it up again, Toshizō
"Sagawa-san,"
called to Sagawa Kanbei, captain of the Aizu clan's Special-Selection corps—a man known for valor even within that clan.

"Judging by how the enemy's guns, great and small, are firing, it looks as though there are not many men in the town quarter off to the west. What do you say we swing wide through the town, come round behind the Gokō-no-miya, and take them between us from north and south?"
"Just so,"
It was the first Sagawa had thought of it. To strike the enemy at his weak point is the very heart of tactics. The Naganuma school has it too.
Toshizō's, though, was the inborn school of the brawl.
"Let's do it,"
and on the spot he gathered the several commanders of the Aizu clan and of the shogunal Denshūtai and made the plan plain to them all.
The vanguard was the Shinsengumi. Having once, at the time of the Hamaguri Gate affair, fought Chōshū troops in the streets of Fushimi, Toshizō stepped forward and took the task upon himself.
In a rush they set off westward.
Coming by way of Hatchō-nawate, they burst into the town quarter; a few Chōshū troops were there, but they were soon scattered.
(We can win.)
Toshizō stood at the corner of Ryōgaemachi-dōri (a north-south street),
"let the Denshūtai advance north up this street,"
he directed, and pressed on further west.
He came out onto Shinmachi-dōri (another north-south street).
"Run north,"
Toshizō charged. Down the narrow street, in columns three and four abreast, came shogunal troops of every kind behind him.
But that lasted twenty meters.
Every last townhouse on either side spat up gunfire all at once. The shogunal men fell one after another.
It was Chōshū's Yūgekitai, the raiding corps.
"Denshūtai, keep running just as you are,"
and leaving that word behind, Toshizō led the Shinsengumi like a gust of wind, falling on the empty houses, fighting the Chōshū troops, smashing them one house at a time as he advanced.
Once it came to street-fighting, to close work, every corpsman worked with a will.
Running further north, they joined the Denshūtai and Aizu troops who had come up ahead of them, and at last got round behind the enemy headquarters, the Gokō-no-miya.
(We've won.)
Toshizō thought once again.
The enemy too seemed taken aback.
The Satsuma army at once sent its crack foot-troops out into the road; first a firefight opened, and before long a fearsome hand-to-hand fight arose.

There was no commanding anything now. Friend and foe fought jammed together in the road. Run, collide with a man, and if he was the enemy you cut him down. It was a melee, like a wash-tub full of taro.
"Shinsengumi, forward! Shinsengumi, forward!"
Toshizō roared, and wherever he saw a strangely-clad figure he cut it down, swept his rear clear, and pressed on. Toward the Gokō-no-miya.
He would climb over its wall.

But by that time the Satsuma gunners under Ōyama Yasuke, who had their battery ranged out on the Ryūunji heights, saw that the fighting was shifting to an unlooked-for quarter and hurriedly began to move their gun-emplacements.
At the same time the Satsuma riflemen too began to concentrate on this quarter and threw up the heaviest net of fire since the fighting had begun.
All about Toshizō the dead and wounded came thick and fast.
The shogunal infantry, and the Denshūtai with them, wavered; but the Aizu troops, true to their name, did not.
Over the dead, and over the dead again, they went cutting their way in.
(Now there is fighting.)
Toshizō was impressed too; only, whenever the Aizu men brought an enemy down, they would without fail cut off his head and hang it at their waists.
At this even Toshizō was at a loss.
Their armor, their battlefield etiquette, their whole art of war—was it not that of three hundred years before?
A head is heavy.
Hang even two heads at your waist and your movements go all a-totter.
In the thick of the melee, whenever Toshizō caught sight of such an Aizu man, he would
"You there, throw that head away,"
bellow at him; but they did not understand him.
The Shinsengumi's hand-to-hand work, by contrast, was lightness itself; but their numbers had dwindled to a startling degree.
Before long the greatest misfortune of the whole Fushimi fight befell the shogunal army.
The building of the Fushimi magistrate's office, their headquarters in the rear, had begun to burn, throwing up showers of sparks.
In a moment the whole neighborhood was lit as bright as noon, and from the Satsuma-Chōshū side the movements of Toshizō and the shogunal army could be read off as plainly as if held in the hand.
The fire of gun and cannon found its mark with precision. To say it poured down like rain would be no exaggeration. And the shogunal army was packed tight into the narrow road.
It was no longer a battle, but a slaughter.
Toshizō was still racing up and down the road directing the fight, and the words he spoke at this moment to the Aizu commander Sagawa Kanbei have been handed down ever since.
"Sagawa-san,"
said Toshizō.
"It seems the wars from here on will have no use for the Hokushin Ittō school or the Tennen Rishin school."
But it was not, from Toshizō, a word of despair.
It was a word full of hope: from now on, he would fight in the Western style.
A strange man.
He seems to have been smiling.
That smiling face was lit by the flames of the Fushimi magistrate's office.
(My true life begins here, from this battlefield.)
Toshizō gathered his corpsmen.
"Are you all here?"
In the rain of bullets he looked over the cluster of faces. Sixty-odd men stood there.
Harada Sanosuke, Nagakura Shinpachi, Saitō Hajime—the hale faces of the unit captains who had been with him since the corps was founded.
But nowhere to be seen was Inoue Genzaburō—elder disciple in the Tennen Rishin school, captain of the Sixth Unit, who had come out with him from their home country. Nor the inspector Yamazaki Susumu.
"And Yamazaki-kun?"
"Wounded, and sent back to the rear."
"And the rest of them?"
There was no need to say. The number gone into the register of the dead was more than a hundred.
"Right—with these sixty we'll push them back once more."
Toshizō sat himself down with a thump.
A bullet grazed the air above his head.
